_note: V1.4b. Sector regulation, as LAWS -- the assembly divides on them, which is why they are here and not in data/company-actions/. Each names one sector and a signed burden on it; src/sim/companies.gd prices that burden in growth and in jobs, both read through the named firms of data/companies/. See docs/companies-model.md.
_cost_and_buy: EVERY law names its losers as well as its winners, and the first draft of this file did not -- which tools/companies_probe.gd table (j) caught. Written on the rule that bloc_offset must not restate a reaction the measured channels already register, the file gave the whole regulation stack +6.45 headline points against a noise floor of 3.0: free approval, and the strictly-dominated shape three previous sessions each hit. The rule was too broad. A saturated burden moves growth by ~0.1 %/yr and unemployment by ~0.02 points, which is BELOW the opinion model's resolution, so the political price of a rule is a fact the measured channels structurally cannot express and has to be authored -- docs/defence-model.md's finding about `defence` being weighted 0.00 by five blocs of six, reached from a second direction.
_weighting: Offsets are set against opinion_constants.BLOC_SIZE, not by eye: workers are 0.30 of the electorate and business 0.10, so a rule that pleases business and costs workers is a net loss however it reads on the row. The full regulation stack is deliberately near approval-NEUTRAL and costs growth, and the full deregulation stack is an approval loss that buys growth. Neither direction is a free opening, which is what table (j) exists to check.
_no_agriculture_deregulation: Deliberate. Agriculture's named payroll is 39k against a 30.9M labour force and its named output is 0.7% of GDP, so both measured channels sit below the readable floor there. A deregulation law on it would buy nothing measurable and cost real approval -- strictly dominated, which is the shape tools/companies_probe.gd table (k) exists to catch. The sector is regulable in one direction only, and that is a property of the content rather than a gap in it.

laws.name: Industrial Emissions Standards
laws.summary: Binding emissions limits on industrial plant, enforced by inspection and fines.

laws.name: Workplace Safety Act
laws.summary: Mandatory safety standards, inspection rights and employer liability on the factory floor.

laws.name: Banking Conduct Rules
laws.summary: Capital requirements, a duty of care to depositors, and a cap on retail lending charges.

laws.name: Competition Enforcement Act
laws.summary: An empowered competition authority with the power to break up dominant firms and block mergers.

laws.name: Farm Standards Act
laws.summary: Animal welfare, pesticide and traceability standards on agricultural production.

laws.name: Industrial Deregulation Act
laws.summary: Repeal of accumulated industrial rules: lighter inspection, faster consent, fewer reporting duties.

laws.name: Financial Services Deregulation
laws.summary: Lighter capital rules and a simplified conduct regime for banks and insurers.

laws.name: Grid Connection Reform
laws.summary: Fast-track connections for new plant, and a connection queue that finally moves.

laws.name: Data Centre Planning Act
laws.summary: Priority consent for data infrastructure and the substations behind it.

laws.name: Short-Let Licensing Act
laws.summary: A licence and an annual nights cap for holiday lets in the cities.

laws.name: Local Preference Procurement Act
laws.summary: Public contracts to prefer domestic suppliers wherever one is able to bid.

laws.name: Retail Hours Liberalisation
laws.summary: Let the shops decide when to open, Sundays included.

laws.name: Insolvency Rescue Reform
laws.summary: Keep firms trading through a restructuring instead of liquidating them at the first hiccup.

laws.name: Platform Commission Cap
laws.summary: Cap what delivery platforms may charge the restaurants they deliver for.

laws.name: Right to Repair Act
laws.summary: Spare parts and repair manuals available for ten years after the last unit sold.

laws.name: Single Market Standards Act
laws.summary: Adopt the Union's product standards wholesale, and keep the market access that comes with them.

laws.name: Planning Liberalisation Act
laws.summary: A presumption in favour of consent, and a statutory clock on every planning decision.

laws.name: Workplace Algorithm Rules
laws.summary: A human being reviews every automated decision about hiring, pay and dismissal.

_domination: Domination is only meaningful BETWEEN LAWS ON ONE SECTOR -- two rules on different sectors are not substitutes, because which sector a rule lands on decides which of the player's own subsidised firms it reaches. Table (k) caught two same-sector pairs. Industry: workplace_safety_act was cheaper than emissions_standards on both costs AND bought more, so emissions was strictly dominated; the two burdens were swapped rather than the offsets retuned, because a safety regime genuinely is the heavier compliance load and the fix should be the one that is also true. Services: banking_conduct_rules cost double competition_enforcement for a buy 0.0009 larger, which is domination inside the rounding; pensioners went from 0.11 to 0.16, so it is now the bigger lever at the worse rate rather than the worse lever outright.
